text.text: Menu by food cost
Most bad service days start before the truck leaves the commissary. A fixed routine means you open on time with everything aboard.
The day before
Check the stop: address, arrival time, power or generator, spot fee, contact.
Build the prep list for the stop from the expected orders and last time's sell-out times.
Confirm staff and who drives.
Check permits in the window: health permit, event permit for that location, insurance certificate if the host asked.
At the commissary
Prep items made and labeled with date and time
Cold items at 41 degrees Fahrenheit or below; hot holding equipment working
Each prep item set to
Loaded
as it goes on the truck
Water tank full; gray water tank empty
Propane checked; spare tank aboard
Generator fueled; oil checked
Cash float, card reader charged, menu board updated
Staffing
Two people can run a small menu; three keeps a long line moving. Whoever leads the stop owns the cash, the temperatures and the close.
Arrival
Park level and legally; leave room for the line and for neighbors.
Set up the generator downwind and away from the line.
Fire extinguisher reachable; first aid kit aboard.
Hand washing station running before any food is touched.
Service
Post sold-out items on the board straight away.
Keep the line moving: one person takes orders and payment, one cooks, one assembles.
Temperatures checked and written down every two hours.
Cash and cards
Start every stop with the same cash float, and make sure the card reader is charged with a spare battery. Most sales are by card now; a dead reader costs more than a dead burner.
Packing list

cells.text: Tongs, spatulas, thermometers, gloves, towels, sanitizer
Boats, foil, napkins, forks, sauce cups, bags
Extinguisher, first aid kit, wheel chocks, cones

text.text: Example
For the Tuesday brewery night the marinated pork is still to prep. The cook starts it first thing so it marinates at least six hours before loading.
The best food can fail in the wrong place. Choose stops with data, not hope, and drop the ones that do not pay.
What makes a good stop
Hungry people with time to wait: breweries, markets, office parks at lunch, festivals.
A host who promotes you on their own channels.
A fee that leaves room for profit, or a sales share instead of a flat fee.
Shade, power and somewhere for guests to sit or stand.
Kinds of stop

cells.text: Evenings and weekends; steady, loyal crowd; often no fee
Morning to early afternoon; big volume; spot fee
Very high volume; high fees; long day

text.text: Judging a stop
Enter sales, orders and food cost after every service. After three visits, compare:
Sales after spot fee
against the target.
Average ticket
: low tickets mean people buy one item; try a combo.
Sold out at
: early sell-outs mean more prep next time.
Weather
: rainy or windy days explain dips; judge on normal days.
Rules of thumb
Three misses on normal-weather days, and the stop comes off the plan.
Never take two stops on one day without two crews.
Keep one regular stop for each weekday so customers know where to find you.
Private events
Private bookings pay a guaranteed amount. Quote with a
sales minimum
: if guests buy less, the host covers the difference. Ask for a deposit to hold the date, and confirm power, parking and the guest count a week before.
Booking stops
Confirm in writing: date, hours, spot location, fee, power, exclusivity (no second taco truck), and the cancellation rule for bad weather.
Example
The Thursday office park lunch made 760 dollars against a 900 target on a windy day, with only 66 orders. One more visit on a calm day decides whether it stays.
A lapsed permit can close the truck on the spot. Track every permit with its expiry and renew early.
What most trucks need

cells.text: Yearly, often with a propane check
State motor vehicle office and carrier

text.text: Rules differ by city and county; check with your local health department.
The renewal routine
Each Monday, open Permits and look at
Days left
Anything under 45 days: start the renewal and set the status to
Renewal due
Book inspections early; inspectors fill up in spring.
When the new permit arrives, update the issued and expiry dates and set
Valid
Keep copies of every permit on the truck and in this workspace.
Event permits
Some events require their own permit or a temporary health permit. Ask the organizer at booking, and add it as a permit with the event date as the expiry.
When something lapses
A permit past its expiry shows under Overdue. Stop serving where that permit applies, call the issuing office the same day, and book the earliest inspection. Note the call on the permit.
Inspection ready, every day
Hand washing sink stocked, hot water working
Food temperatures logged
Food covered and raised off the floor
Sanitizer at the right strength
Permits displayed where customers can see them
Example

The vending licence expires in 25 days and liability insurance in five. The propane certification already lapsed four days ago, so the truck does not run until the fire marshal signs it off. Both are marked Renewal due; the insurance renewal goes first because a market organizer has asked for a current certificate.
The close sets up the next day. Done well, the truck is clean, the numbers are in, and nothing spoils overnight.
On site
Last orders called; sold-out items posted
Generator off and cooled before packing
Trash and recycling bagged; the spot left cleaner than found
Gray water held for proper disposal, never dumped on site
Back at the commissary
Unload food; cool hot food quickly and label it with the date, or throw it out.
Clean and sanitize every surface, the flat top, the fryer and the hood filters.
Empty gray water; refill fresh water.
Charge the card reader; count cash.
Money
Cash is counted by two people and bagged with the stop name and total. Card totals are checked against the sales report before the stop is closed.
The numbers
Enter on the stop the same night:
Sales
and
Orders
Food cost
for what was used
Weather
Sold out at
for any item that ran out
Then set the stop to
Served
Waste and leftovers

cells.text: Cooled within two hours; used within three days, or thrown out
Labeled; used within the time on the label
Kept dry and sealed; used the next day

text.text: Stops not closed out
A stop whose date has passed but is still Planned or Confirmed shows under Overdue. Enter its numbers or mark it rained out the next morning, so the monthly comparison stays honest.
Weekly truck care
Deep clean the hood and filters
Check tires, lights and brakes
Service the generator by its hour meter
Check propane lines for leaks with soapy water
Example
After the Sunday brewery patio, pork sold out by 4:15 and 131 orders came through. The prep par for that stop goes up and the leftover salsa is labeled for Tuesday.
A food truck is a restaurant that moves every day. Where you park, what you prep and which permits are current decide whether a day makes money. This workspace keeps all three in view.
The lists

cells.text: Each service: place, kind, date, sales target, sales, orders, average ticket, spot fee, food cost and percent, weather, when it sold out, prep loaded
Each item: price, cost per serving, food cost percent, sold per stop
Health permit, licences, fire inspection, commissary agreement, insurance, event permits, with expiry and days left
What the commissary prepares for each stop, by whom, and whether it is loaded
Private events: date, guests, quote, sales minimum, deposit and who pays

text.text: How the numbers work
Average ticket
is sales divided by orders.
Food cost
on a stop is what you spent on food for that service; the percent is against sales. Most trucks aim for 28 to 32 percent.
Sales after spot fee
is what the stop really brought in before labor and fuel.
Your first week
Enter your menu with price and cost per serving.
Add every permit with its expiry date and the office that issues it.
Plan the next two weeks of stops with a sales target for each.
After each service, enter sales, orders, food cost, weather and the time you sold out.
The weekly rhythm
Sunday:
plan next week's stops; confirm with breweries and markets.
Day before each stop:
prep list for the commissary; generator fueled, propane checked.
After each stop:
numbers entered; prep loaded status reset.
Monthly:
look at sales by stop kind and weather; drop stops that miss target three times.
Example
Last Saturday's market sold out of brisket by 12:40 on a hot day with an average ticket around 12 dollars. For this Saturday, the cook smokes 20 more portions and the agua fresca batch is doubled.
